title: Dictionaries and sets
summary: Look values up by key with a dictionary, give a safe default with .get(), and remove duplicates with a set.
objectives: Store and look up key-value pairs in a dictionary
Use .get() with a default so a missing key does not crash the program
Remove duplicates from a list with a set

segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

A dictionary stores pairs: a key (like a name) and a value (like a phone number), so you can look up a value by its key. A set stores each item only once, which makes it the quickest way to remove duplicates. In this lab you build a small contact book, add a person, look up a number with square brackets, and use `.get()` with a default so that asking for a name that is not there gives `not found` instead of an error. Then you take a list of email sign-ups with repeats, turn it into a set, and show that the count drops once the duplicates are gone.

segments.title: Lab: contact book and sign-up list

lab.title: Contact book and sign-up list
lab.objective: Build a dictionary contact book with safe .get() lookups, then use a set to count unique email sign-ups.
lab.instructions:
Part 1: the contact book. The dictionary contacts maps names to phone numbers.

1. Add a third contact: the key "Chloe" with the value "555-0103".
2. Look up Ben's number with square brackets, contacts["Ben"], and print it as: Ben: 555-0102
3. Look up "Dev" (who is not in the book) with .get() and the default "not found", and print it as: Dev: not found

Part 2: the sign-ups. The list signups holds six email addresses, some repeated.

4. Make a set from the list with set(signups) and store it in unique_signups.
5. Print how many sign-ups there were and how many are unique, as two lines: Sign-ups: 6 and Unique: 3. Use len() for both numbers.

Your program should print exactly four lines:

Ben: 555-0102
Dev: not found
Sign-ups: 6
Unique: 3
lab.constraints: Keep the variable names contacts, signups and unique_signups. Do not change the signups list. Use .get() with a default for Dev; do not use if or try. Use len() to count; do not type 6 or 3 yourself. Do not use input().
lab.starter_code:
# Part 1: a contact book (name -> phone number)
contacts = {
    "Asha": "555-0101",
    "Ben": "555-0102",
}

# 1. Add "Chloe" with the number "555-0103"

# 2. Print Ben's number using square brackets, like:  Ben: 555-0102

# 3. Print Dev's number using .get() with the default "not found", like:  Dev: not found

# Part 2: email sign-ups with duplicates
signups = ["asha@mail.com", "ben@mail.com", "asha@mail.com", "chloe@mail.com", "ben@mail.com", "asha@mail.com"]

# 4. Make a set from signups and store it in unique_signups

# 5. Print the two counts, like:  Sign-ups: 6  and  Unique: 3
hints: Add to a dictionary with square brackets: contacts["Chloe"] = "555-0103". Read with square brackets too: contacts["Ben"].
contacts.get("Dev", "not found") gives the number if Dev is there and "not found" if not. A set is made with set(signups); it keeps one copy of each address.
Print with commas: print("Ben:", contacts["Ben"]), print("Dev:", contacts.get("Dev", "not found")), print("Sign-ups:", len(signups)) and print("Unique:", len(unique_signups)).

lab.solution:
contacts = {
    "Asha": "555-0101",
    "Ben": "555-0102",
}

contacts["Chloe"] = "555-0103"

print("Ben:", contacts["Ben"])
print("Dev:", contacts.get("Dev", "not found"))

signups = ["asha@mail.com", "ben@mail.com", "asha@mail.com", "chloe@mail.com", "ben@mail.com", "asha@mail.com"]

unique_signups = set(signups)

print("Sign-ups:", len(signups))
print("Unique:", len(unique_signups))
